title: Why does @Transactional on private method do nothing? Why does @Async self-invoke run synchronously? How do you propagate tx/security context to @Async? What is JIT? How do sessions work in stateless REST? What are coding best practices? How do you migrate to serverless?
shortTitle: Why does @Transactional on private method do nothing?
keyPoints: @Transactional on a private method is silently ignored because CGLIB cannot override private methods -- the proxy never intercepts the call.
Self-invocation (calling this.method()) bypasses the proxy entirely, so @Transactional and @Async annotations on the called method are ignored.
The clean fix is extracting the annotated method into a separate @Service bean so the call passes through that bean's proxy.
SecurityContext, MDC, and TransactionContext are ThreadLocal and do not propagate to @Async worker threads -- use TaskDecorator or DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor.
JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler converts frequently executed bytecode into native machine code for peak performance -- C1 compiles quickly, C2 optimizes aggressively.
Stateless REST APIs use JWT tokens instead of HttpSession, with no server-side session state between requests.
Spring Cloud Function lets you deploy banking logic as a serverless function on AWS Lambda with the same Spring programming model.

s1_definition.oneliner: Private methods are invisible to the CGLIB proxy, self-invocation via this bypasses the proxy, @Async threads lose ThreadLocal context, and the fix for all proxy issues is to call through a separate bean.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **CGLIB proxy** -- Spring creates a subclass of your bean that overrides public methods to add transactional or async behavior; private methods cannot be overridden, so they are never intercepted.
- **Self-invocation** -- when a method inside a bean calls another method on the same bean using `this`, the call goes directly to the real object, bypassing the proxy wrapper.
- **ThreadLocal context loss** -- SecurityContext, MDC (logging correlation), and TransactionContext are stored in ThreadLocal, which is tied to the current thread; @Async runs on a different thread that starts with empty ThreadLocal.
- **TaskDecorator** -- a callback that wraps each Runnable submitted to a ThreadPoolTaskExecutor, allowing you to copy context from the caller thread to the worker thread.
- **JIT compiler** -- the JVM's Just-In-Time compiler that detects hot methods and compiles them from bytecode to native machine code for faster execution.
- **Spring Cloud Function** -- a framework that lets you write business logic as a plain Java Function and deploy it to AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, or Google Cloud Functions.
s1_definition.analogy: The CCTV camera at National Bank of India sits at the entrance of each department. When Priya (a customer) walks through the entrance to see a teller, the camera records the visit. But if one teller calls a colleague at the same desk (self-invocation), the camera does not see it because the call never passes through the entrance. The fix: send the colleague to a different department (separate @Service bean) so the call passes through that department's camera (proxy).

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spring AOP has two critical pitfalls that silently corrupt data. First, @Transactional on a private method is ignored because CGLIB creates a subclass proxy, and Java does not allow subclasses to override private methods. Second, calling a @Transactional or @Async method from within the same class via this bypasses the proxy because the call goes directly to the real object. At National Bank of India, Rajesh fixes both by extracting the annotated method into a separate @Service bean so every call passes through the proxy.

The third pitfall is ThreadLocal context loss. SecurityContext, MDC, and TransactionContext do not transfer to @Async worker threads. Rajesh registers an MdcTaskDecorator on the ThreadPoolTaskExecutor that captures the MDC map from the request thread and restores it on the worker thread. For SecurityContext, he wraps the executor with DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor. The async notification runs on a dedicated bounded pool -- never the default SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor, which creates unlimited threads.

Remember one sentence: the proxy sits at the entrance, so call through a separate bean, never through this, and carry ThreadLocal context with a TaskDecorator.
